item.title: Bridging the Knowledge Gap in Federated Prompt Learning via Text-Guided Feature Augmentation
item.description:
ACM MM · Yibin Wang, Yucan Zhou, Hongcheng Li, Zenghao Guan, Xiaoyan Gu, Weiping Wang
Federated Prompt Learning (FPL) is a communication-efficient paradigm for collaboratively fine-tuning Vision-Language Models (VLMs). However, FPL suffers from performance degradation under data heterogeneity. While existing methods primarily improve personalization capability, the aggregated global model still suffers from degradation due to imbalanced local knowledge. To tackle this challenge, we propose Federated prompt learning via Text-Guided Augmentation (FedTGA), a novel framework that leverages the shared text modality of VLMs as a semantic bridge for privacy-aware cross-client knowledge sharing. Through Text-bridged Prototype Estimation (TPE) and Attribute-based Diversity Sharing (ADS), FedTGA enables both inter-class knowledge complementation and fine-grained diversity sharing. Specifically, the TPE module utilizes cross-modal structural similarity to collaboratively estimate visual prototypes of unfamiliar classes without exposing local prototypes, and ADS leverages textual attributes to aggregate and transfer fine-grained visual variations across clients to enhance intra-class diversity. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FedTGA serves as an effective and orthogonal module, consistently and significantly boosting the global performance of various FPL methods across diverse non-IID settings.

item.title: Correlation-Guided Latent Sharing for Non-IID Federated Learning
item.description:
CIKM · Mahran Jazi, Sharva Gogawale, Irad Ben-Gal
Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training across distributed clients without centralizing raw data, but its performance often degrades under non-independent and non-identically distributed (non-IID) data. This degradation is especially severe when clients observe only a limited subset of the global label space, causing biased local updates and client drift. Standard aggregation methods such as FedAvg and FedProx mainly address this problem at the optimization level, but they do not directly enrich the incomplete local data distributions that cause heterogeneity. This paper proposes Correlation-Guided Latent Sharing (CGLS), a federated learning framework that selectively augments client training using latent information received from statistically aligned peers. CGLS identifies compatible clients through gradient-direction correlation and mixes local training data with synthetic latent information from correlated neighbors. We formulate this process as a mixed-distribution federated objective and explain how targeted mixing can reduce gradient dispersion under severe label skew. Experiments on MNIST, FashionMNIST and CIFAR-10 under Dirichlet and balanced one-class non-IID partitions show that CGLS improves accuracy and macro-F1 over FedAvg and FedProx, with the largest gains appearing in the strongest heterogeneity settings.

item.title: Knowledge-Driven Recommendations in Decentralized Systems: Integrating Federated Personal Data and Public Contexts
item.description:
CIKM · Fernando Spadea
Modern recommendation systems force a critical trade-off between user data sovereignty and algorithmic personalization, while decentralized alternatives often struggle with data sparsity and reactive interventions that fail during high-volatility events, like decentralized finance liquidations. This doctoral research outlines a comprehensive framework that bridges sovereignty-preserving collaborative learning with predictive risk management. By fusing private personal knowledge graphs with public contextual data through computationally efficient retrieval-augmented generation and federated learning, the system generates highly tailored recommendations without exposing raw user data. Concurrently, it develops proactive, agentic architectures utilizing Survival Analysis and the physics of self-organized criticality to forecast individual time-to-event risks and systemic network fragility. By integrating these macroscopic and microscopic topological signals, the framework empowers automated agents to dynamically shift from yield-maximizing recommendations to minimally invasive, protective interventions, safeguarding users against cascading failures in decentralized ecosystems.

item.title: Progressive Collaboration Pruning for Federated Learning
item.description:
CIKM · Siyao Cheng, Boyi Liu, Zimu Zhou, Zheng Wu, Yongxin Tong
Collaboration-based personalized federated learning (Co-PFL) mitigates data heterogeneity by enabling clients to selectively exchange knowledge through a learned collaboration graph. Despite their success, existing Co-PFL methods often update collaboration weights mainly from pairwise similarity, which can produce graphs that are either overly sparse and hinder knowledge propagation or overly dense and weaken personalization, leaving graph connectivity largely uncontrolled. In this paper, we propose FedPGP, a Co-PFL framework that explicitly schedules collaboration from dense to sparse over training rounds, enabling clients to first exploit broadly shared knowledge and then refine specialized knowledge aligned with their local distributions. FedPGP builds on a connectivity-aware similarity regularization that jointly accounts for global graph connectivity and client-model similarity, together with an efficient greedy pruning rule that removes edges with the least contribution to the regularized objective. We further present FedPGP+, a module-specific extension that learns different collaboration graphs for different model modules, allowing collaboration intensity to vary along model depth. Extensive experiments across diverse non-IID settings show that FedPGP and FedPGP+ consistently outperform state-of-the-art Co-PFL baselines, achieving up to 5.52% absolute accuracy improvement, while producing interpretable dense-to-sparse collaboration schedules.

item.title: Release the Potential of Relative Feature Consistency for Data Heterogeneous Federated Learning
item.description:
CIKM · Yibin Wang, Yucan Zhou, Xiaoyan Gu, Hongcheng Li, Jiang Zhou, Weiping Wang
Federated Learning is a promising paradigm to achieve privacy-preserving collaborative training. However, its performance degrades severely under data heterogeneity. A main obstacle is the divergent local representations induced by data heterogeneity, which will degrade the quality of the aggregated global representations. In this paper, we discover that although local representation spaces contain client-specific biases, their internal inter-class structure remains consistent across clients, which we identify as relative consistency. Through theoretical and empirical analyses, we further show that a proxy dataset can serve as a common anchor to translate class prototypes into a relative space, where client-specific shifts are suppressed and cross-client class centers become better aligned. Based on these findings, we propose a novel framework named Federated learning with Relative Representation Alignment (FedReRA) with Relative Knowledge Extraction (RKE) and Relative Ensemble Inference (REI) to extract and leverage the relative consistency to address data heterogeneity. Specifically, RKE debiases the prototypes by translating absolute prototypes into the aligned relative space via a flexible proxy dataset, while REI conducts collaborative inference with bias-reduced prediction in the relative space. Extensive experiments validate FedReRA's superiority over state-of-the-art methods, achieving a 3.83% average improvement under high heterogeneity and notably sustaining nearly 10% improvement on CIFAR-100 even when using random noise as the proxy data.

item.title: When Geometry Becomes Unreliable: Robust Federated Aggregation via Bounded Influence
item.description:
CIKM · Yitong Ma, Gang Yan
Robust aggregation in federated learning is often framed as down-weighting abnormal client updates. However, in realistic cross-device regimes, each round observes only a small number of high-dimensional updates, while benign updates can already be anisotropic, heavy-tailed, and strongly affected by non-IID data. In this setting, robustness depends not only on the final weighting rule, but also on whether the server-visible update geometry is estimable. We propose FedBIG (Federated Bounded-Influence Geometry), a server-side aggregation framework that separates geometry construction from influence control. Instead of scoring raw updates directly, FedBIG builds a stabilized sketch-space geometry using robust centering, low-dimensional projection, calibrated scatter estimation, shrinkage, and whitening. It then maps stabilized deviations to bounded-influence weights and aggregates the original client updates. Experiments on heterogeneous federated learning benchmarks show that FedBIG improves the robustness--utility trade-off under statistical and triggered poisoning. Ablations, boundary stress tests, and runtime analysis further support the central claim: robust aggregation is effective when server-visible geometry is estimable, and weakens when this geometry collapses under extreme heterogeneity or sparse participation. Our code is available at https://github.com/ytma-phoenix/FedBIG.

item.title: When Is Shallow Enough? Adaptive Split Federated Learning with Client-Specific Sufficiency Estimation
item.description:
CIKM · Wenhao Yuan, Chenchen Lin, Wentao Hu, Jian Chen, Jinfeng Xu, Shujie Li
Split Federated Learning (SFL) enables distributed model training by splitting networks between the server and clients. However, under client heterogeneity, the conventional static split strategy may be suboptimal because clients can differ in data distributions, adaptation dynamics, and representation learning progress, making a single split point insufficient to accommodate client-specific training states. In this paper, we propose FedSGA , a S ufficiency- G uided A daptive split Fed erated learning framework that addresses this question through client-specific shallow sufficiency estimation. First, we introduce a client-specific adaptation channel based on private prompt tokens, which tracks local adaptation dynamics separately from the shared backbone and provides a lightweight signal for detecting whether client adaptation remains active. To further avoid repeated online probing over multiple candidate depths, we design a shallow sufficiency estimator that combines cross-client semantic alignment, temporal interface stability, and prompt-state variation to estimate whether the shallowest split is already sufficient. Finally, we introduce a split-compatible interface harmonization module that projects activations from different split depths into a shared semantic space, improving the comparability of heterogeneous client interfaces before server-side prediction. Extensive experiments on multiple heterogeneous benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of FedSGA in improving model performance compared with state-of-the-art methods while reducing unnecessary client-side computation.

item.title: FedCSOT: Model-Heterogeneous Personalized Federated Learning via Channel Semantic Optimal Transport
item.description:
CIKM · Yiheng Li, Huan Zhou, Xiuhua Li, Yuanchao Shu
Federated Learning (FL) provides a privacy-preserving paradigm for collaborative learning across distributed clients. In practical FL systems, clients often exhibit non-IID data distributions and deploy diverse model architectures under resource constraints. While model heterogeneity improves deployment flexibility under client resource constraints, it prevents direct parameter aggregation and makes cross-architecture knowledge transfer challenging. Existing methods mainly rely on shared structures, coarse-grained distillation, or projection-based feature alignment, which cannot explicitly capture channel-level semantic correspondences across heterogeneous architectures. This paper proposes FedCSOT, a model-heterogeneous personalized FL framework based on channel semantic optimal transport. FedCSOT induces sequence-driven channel semantics from channel responses over a shared unlabeled sequence, establishing a common semantic space for cross-architecture alignment. The framework models cross-architecture semantic alignment through entropy-regularized optimal transport to facilitate knowledge transfer. It further designs a divergence-aware personalized fusion strategy to adaptively balance consensus knowledge and local personalization under non-IID data distributions. Extensive experiments under diverse data and model heterogeneity settings demonstrate that FedCSOT consistently improves average test accuracy, convergence behavior, and robustness over representative baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/greenhead01/FedCSOT.

item.title: FUCH: Non-IID Federated Unlearning via Classification-layer Hybrid-order Constraints
item.description:
CIKM · Tengyuan He, Yunfei Zi, Yuelong Xia, Lin Liu, Shaojie Qiao, Mingjing Tang
Federated unlearning (FU) aims to support the ''right to be forgotten'' by reducing the influence of target samples without full retraining. However, when applied to deep neural networks (DNNs) in practical non-IID scenarios, existing FU methods suffer from low unlearning efficiency and deviate from the retraining reference's predictive behavior. Specifically, they require costly full-model updates or multi-round communication, failing to disentangle the complex coupling of target-sample influence and retained knowledge. In this work, we revisit the necessity of full-model updates for sample-level FU and investigate the formation of this complex coupling. We reveal key empirical insights: (1) updating solely the final classification layer can effectively approximate the predictive behavior of full retraining; and (2) disentangling target-sample influence under non-IID settings requires separately resolving distinct intra-client and cross-client knowledge couplings. Based on these insights, we propose FUCH, a classification-layer-based hybrid-order-constrained FU framework. To improve unlearning efficiency, FUCH freezes the feature extractor and performs a single-round update on the final classification layer. Furthermore, to disentangle the complex knowledge coupling, FUCH employs a coupling-aware hybrid-order mechanism combining local second-order and global first-order information to constrain the unlearning updates. Extensive experiments across diverse non-IID benchmarks validate our empirical insights and demonstrate that FUCH achieves efficient unlearning while significantly outperforming SOTA baselines in closely approximating the retraining reference's predictive behavior.

item.title: Towards Efficient Federated Time Series Forecasting under Structural Data Heterogeneity across Nodes
item.description:
CIKM · Yiming Zhou, Jiahao Wang, Mingyue Cheng, Hao Wang, Defu Lian, Enhong Chen
Time series data is highly valuable yet sharing-sensitive across nodes, making federated learning a promising paradigm to leverage distributed temporal data. However, varying sampling standards lead to heterogeneous data structures across nodes, with diverse time granularities and inconsistent variable sets being particularly prominent, posing significant challenges for conventional federated learning frameworks. In this paper, we propose PiXTime, a novel Transformer-based time series forecasting model designed to tolerate and exploit such structurally heterogeneous distributed data. Specifically, we redesign the internal modules and adopt the parameter-decoupling philosophy by carefully designating each module as either local or shared to handle the unique challenges of the federated scenario. To address granularity misalignments, PiXTime retains a personalized set of local modules for each node, acting as a crucial bridge between the node-specific raw temporal granularities and the unified feature dimension of the federated network. To tackle variable inconsistencies, we design a shared VE Table that explicitly injects globally unified variable categorical identities into specific auxiliary tokens, enhancing PiXTime's capability to collaboratively train under highly diverse auxiliary variable distributions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PiXTime not only establishes state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance in handling structurally heterogeneous distributed data but also achieves superiority in conventional benchmarks. We open-source our code at https://github.com/WearTheClo/PiXTime.

item.title: FDA-Opt: Federated Fine-Tuning via Dynamic Update Schedules
item.description:
CIKM · Michael Theologitis, Vasilis Samoladas, Antonios Deligiannakis
Federated Learning (FL) enables the utilization of vast, previously inaccessible data sources. At the same time, pre-trained Language Models (LMs) have taken the world by storm and for good reason. They exhibit remarkable emergent abilities and are readily adapted to downstream tasks. This opens one of the most exciting frontiers in FL: fine-tuning LMs. Yet, a persistent challenge in FL is the frequent, rigid communication of parameters—a problem magnified by the sheer size of these contemporary models. The FedOpt family of algorithms has become the go-to approach for FL, relying on fixed but arbitrary intervals for model exchanges. Recently, the FDA algorithm prescribed a dynamic approach by monitoring the training progress. However, it introduced a hard-to-calibrate parameter and imposed a rigid synchronization scheme. In this work, we address these limitations by proposing the FDA-Opt family of algorithms—a unified generalization of both FDA and FedOpt. Our experimental evaluation focuses on fine-tuning LMs on downstream NLP tasks and demonstrates that FDA-Opt outperforms FedOpt even when it is configured with hyper-parameters specifically optimized for the latter. In other words, we show that FDA-Opt is a practical, drop-in replacement for FedOpt in modern FL libraries and systems: it requires no additional configuration and delivers superior performance out of the box.

item.title: Transcending the Semantic Chasm: Knowledge-Graph Guided Aggregation for Cross-Silo Federated Session Recommendation
item.description:
CIKM · Changjie Wang, Bohan Li, Wenlong Wu, Meng Ma, Yuanyang Zhang, Yuhang Dai
Session-based Recommendation (SBR) achieves high performance in traditional centralized settings by using global item transition graphs to capture user intent. However, Federated Learning (FL) mandates collaborative training on isolated data, which makes the construction of such global structures unattainable. We identify this critical dilemma as ''Structure Collapse'', where the global graph remains fragmented despite model averaging. This collapse induces a ''Semantic Chasm,'' resulting in incompatible knowledge fusion and imprecise intent prediction. To break this impasse, we propose a novel Cross-Silo Federated Session-based Recommendation framework (CSFSR), which reconstructs global connectivity by harmonizing knowledge priors with local intents. Specifically, our Knowledge-Aware Initialization counteracts Structure Collapse by synthesizing shared attributes into a unified semantic space that anchors isolated clients. Further addressing the Semantic Chasm, the Graph-Guided Aggregation mechanism uses client signatures to direct personalized fusion, effectively filtering noise and ensuring robustness. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that CSFSR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art federated baselines and exhibits superior noise robustness. Our code is available at https://github.com/Is-Jiejie/CSFSR.

item.title: Fair to Federate? Two-Sided Prediction of Performance and Fairness Outcomes in Healthcare Federated Learning
item.description:
CIKM · Marina Ceccon, Alessandro Fabris, Ornella Irrera, Gianmaria Silvello, Gian Antonio Susto
Federated learning (FL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for collaborative healthcare modeling under privacy constraints, yet institutions currently lack tools to anticipate how joining a federation will impact predictive performance and fairness. Existing work has primarily focused on post-hoc fairness mitigation, while overlooking the pre-collaboration decision itself. In this work, we introduce the Federation Assessment Problem, a two-sided prediction problem concerned with anticipating how federation would affect both a candidate institution seeking to join a federation and the institutions already participating in it, before collaboration occurs. To address this problem, we propose a two-stage meta-learning framework that predicts changes in performance and fairness metrics from institution-level metadata. We evaluate the framework on two healthcare imaging domains, across federations of varying sizes. Results show that federation-induced changes in both predictive performance and fairness can be estimated with high accuracy. The analysis further identifies label bias as one of the strongest predictors of fairness outcomes across both domains, often rivaling or exceeding demographic composition in importance. These findings demonstrate that informed federation assessment is possible without raw data sharing and highlight the need to explicitly measure multiple sources of bias when reasoning about fairness in healthcare FL.

item.title: FedMem: Memory-Aware Federated Continual Learning via Dual-Channel Memory Control
item.description:
CIKM · Shiyang Li, Yuan Ma, Weining Weng, Yuchen Liu, Qianzhong Chen, Yiqiang Chen
Federated continual learning (FCL) suffers from complex spatio-temporal catastrophic forgetting, driven by distribution drift along task streams and aggregation conflicts under non-IID client data. Existing studies often treat temporal and spatial forgetting as decoupled objectives, overlooking their interaction in the overall memory dynamics of the federation, where client-side acquisition and server-side consolidation jointly shape long-term performance. Motivated by the structural and functional correspondence between the dual-channel memory mechanism in collective cognition and FCL's client-server collaboration, we introduce Federated System Memory (FSM), a system memory metric that jointly models client-side short-term retention and server-side long-term consistency. Based on FSM, we further propose FedMem, a memory-aware FCL framework that utilizes dual-channel memory control to enable system-level closed-loop optimization. On the client side, FedMem constrains local learning with dual-channel decay indicators: short-term decay strengthens prototype-based retention, while long-term decay enhances memory-guided regularization for stable task-memory retrieval. On the server side, it regulates global updates through collective-consistency gated aggregation and adaptive update scaling based on long-term decay, while maintaining global prototypes and memory. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FedMem consistently outperforms existing methods in both learning performance and system memory retention.

item.title: Backdoor Poisoning Mitigation for Federated LoRA via Structural Adaptive Control
item.description:
CIKM · Wenhan Hu, Zhe Wang, Gang Yan
Large pre-trained models are increasingly adapted on user devices, but direct fine-tuning in federated settings is constrained by computation, memory, and communication limits. These constraints have motivated the use of parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods, among which LoRA is widely adopted by concentrating adaptation in low-rank parameters. While this design improves efficiency, it also changes the security setting. In federated LoRA, backdoor behavior can exploit the low-rank adaptation structure and persist across communication rounds, making defenses designed for full-model updates less reliable. To address this gap, we propose StrAP, a server-side defense tailored to federated LoRA fine-tuning. StrAP combines reliability control before aggregation with structure-aware regulation after aggregation. Before aggregation, client updates are softly weighted based on their alignment with a clean validation gradient and tracked across rounds using a stateful trust mechanism, which suppresses persistent anomalies while allowing benign recovery. After aggregation, StrAP analyzes the LoRA parameter structure to identify suspicious rank channels using robust cross-client statistics and applies utility-calibrated structural actions guided by clean validation loss. Extensive experiments show that StrAP consistently reduces backdoor attack success rates with minimal impact on clean accuracy. Our code is available at https://github.com/HwhCN-ui/StrAP.

item.title: CRAFT: Cross-Region Adaptive Federated Transfer Learning for Urban Spatiotemporal Prediction
item.description:
CIKM · Zhehao Dai, Xiao Han, Zhaolin Deng, Xuyuan Hu, Zijian Zhang, Guojiang Shen
Urban spatiotemporal prediction is crucial for smart city management, yet fragmented data across administrative boundaries significantly impedes effective model training. To overcome data limitations and leverage knowledge from data-rich regions while preserving data privacy, federated transfer learning has emerged as a promising approach for cross-regional urban prediction tasks. However, traditional learning methods encounter the dual challenge: (1) intra-regional knowledge acquisition difficulties due to missing boundaries that weaken spatiotemporal dependencies and cause data sparsity; and (2) cross-regional knowledge transfer bias, where distribution differences between source and target regions trigger negative transfer and reduce model robustness. To address these issues, we propose CRAFT: a novel federated transfer learning framework that integrates Large Language Models (LLMs) for urban spatiotemporal prediction. Leveraging LLMs' powerful semantic understanding and contextual reasoning abilities, CRAFT captures complex spatiotemporal dependencies and uncovers latent regional connections from heterogeneous data sources, thus alleviating boundary-induced data sparsity. Additionally, to address inter-regional data heterogeneity, we employ a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model with parameter decoupling, which excels at handling diverse data distributions while minimizing federated communication costs. Experimental results on real-world datasets from multiple cities demonstrate the effectiveness of CRAFT in cross-regional federated transfer learning. The code is publicly available at: https://github.com/Jasonxx4/CRAFT.

item.title: Federated Personalization of Early-Exit Networks
item.description:
CIKM · Boyi Liu, Zimu Zhou, Cheng Fang, Yongxin Tong
Personalized Federated Learning (PFL) excels at tailoring client specific models, which is particularly critical for decentralized and heterogeneous data environments, yet existing methods produce static models with a fixed tradeoff between accuracy and efficiency. This inherent static nature limits their ability to adapt to inference demands that vary with context and resource availability, posing a challenge for real-world deployment. Early-exit networks (EENs), which enable adaptive inference via intermediate classifiers, offer a promising solution. However, integrating EENs into PFL introduces two intertwined conflicts: client-wise heterogeneity across clients and depth-wise interference arising from conflicting exit objectives. Prior studies fail to resolve both conflicts simultaneously, leading to suboptimal performance. In this paper, we propose X-FED, a novel Conflict-Aware Cross-Client Federated Exit Distillation framework that jointly addresses both client- and depth-wise conflicts while extending PFL to early-exit networks. At its core, X-FED employs a progressive, depth-prioritized student coordination mechanism that mitigates interference among shallow and deep exits while enabling effective personalized knowledge transfer across clients. Furthermore, we introduce a client-decoupled formulation that reduces communication overhead with theoretical soundness. Extensive evaluations on various datasets show that compared to state-of-the-art PFL and PFL-EE methods, X-FED achieves higher accuracy while reducing inference costs by 30.79%–46.86%.

item.title: DICE: Decentralized Incentive-driven Federated Learning for Efficient & Scalable Customization of Pretrained Models in Web3
item.description:
CIKM · Hong Lin, Zhongle Xie, Lidan Shou, Ke Chen, Gang Chen
Customizing Pretrained Models (PMs) for downstream tasks demands task-specific data, which burgeoning Web3 applications provide abundantly. Blockchain-powered federated learning (BCFL) offers a secure and privacy-preserving paradigm to customize PMs among self-interested and untrusted Web3 participants. Yet, existing BCFL algorithms face severe efficiency and scalability challenges when applied to large PMs, due to their substantial computational and memory requirements and the hardware constraints of many participants. This paper introduces DICE, a novel BCFL algorithm that addresses the efficiency and scalability challenges of customizing large PMs in Web3 via two sets of synergistic techniques: (i) a dynamic progressive learning scheme and a model slice verification scheme to enable a wider range of honest participants, including those unable to deploy the full model, to engage in customizing PMs, while preserving model utility; (ii) a tree-structured committee consensus protocol and an efficiency-driven incentive scheme to address the dominant bottleneck that hinders existing BCFL algorithms from scaling to a larger number of data holders for customizing data-hungry large PMs, while maintaining security. Theoretical analysis and extensive experimental results on customizing vision and language PMs demonstrate DICE 's efficiency, effectiveness, and security. A comprehensive technical report of DICE including its implementation details, extended analyses, discussions, and experiments is available at https://github.com/Hoho-Lin/DICE.

item.title: HiMAC: Hierarchical Federated Learning with Mobility-Aware Collaboration
item.description:
CIKM · Yibo Pan, Boyi Liu, Zimu Zhou, Fan Gao, Tianyi Wang, Yi Xu
Mobility-aware hierarchical federated learning (MobiHFL) is an emerging paradigm to support urban applications where clients continuously move across edge-server coverage areas. Existing methods mainly treat mobility as a scheduling challenge and often train a single global model across all edge-servers. This overlooks the spatial non-IID characteristics of urban environments, where regions exhibit distinct yet correlated data distributions. Region-wise personalization is a natural remedy, but mobility makes it difficult. Each edge model is trained on its current client population, while future arriving and departing clients may follow different distributions, causing cold-start degradation and feature-classifier mismatch after handover. We propose \sysname, a personalized MobiHFL framework that turns predicted client movement into proactive inter-edge collaboration. \sysname uses per-client LSTM trajectory predictors to estimate future client flows and builds a round-level transition matrix to guide collaboration. With a decoupled backbone-classifier architecture, \sysname prepares each edge for expected incoming clients through incoming-aware classifier initialization and improves compatibility with likely destination edges through outgoing-regularized backbone training. Extensive experiments on image classification and object detection benchmarks show improvements of up to 12.18 percentage points in image-classification accuracy and 6.50 points in mAP@50 over state-of-the-art baselines across varying mobility intensities.

item.title: ProRC: Prototype Personalization with Reliability Calibration in Heterogeneous Federated Learning
item.description:
CIKM · Yanchao Tang, Baoyao Yang, Yuhao Chen, Chenxiang Zhao
Prototype-based federated learning (FL) provides a promising route for federated heterogeneity. By exchanging class prototypes rather than model parameters, it provides class-level semantic guidance under non-IID data and accommodates heterogeneous client backbones. Under severely skewed label distributions, however, two coupled limitations emerge. The broadcast global prototype is a cross-client average, and direct adoption can cause client semantic dilution. Meanwhile, local prototypes of rare classes are estimated from a few samples, leading to local margin erosion against well-supported neighbours. To address both, we propose ProRC, a prototype personalization framework grounded in shrinkage estimation. ProRC replaces naive alignment with a reliability-calibrated, margin-aware interpolation between global and local prototypes, and comprises two complementary client-side modules. The first module, Reliability-Calibrated Prototype Adaptation (RaPA), calibrates each global prototype by the reliability of its local counterpart, restoring client-specific semantics only to the extent the data warrant. The second module, Margin-Aware Prototype Refinement (MaPR), audits the candidate against the local true-class margin and attenuates margin-reducing steps. Together, the two modules are designed to mitigate client semantic dilution and local margin erosion, while preserving the prototype-exchange protocol and per-round payload of prior methods. Extensive experiments on label-skewed and real-world image benchmarks, together with ablation and reliability analyses, show that ProRC achieves the best overall average accuracy among the compared methods and improves the strongest prototype baseline in most heterogeneous settings.

item.title: FedEMoE: Towards Class-Aware Federated Learning via Evidential Mixture-of-Experts
item.description:
CIKM · Linbo Zhou, Weishan Zhang, Tao Chen, Lingzhao Meng
Federated learning under non-IID data suffers from client drift. Recent work introduces Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures to handle data heterogeneity by routing inputs to specialized experts, but two problems remain. Softmax routing produces overconfident expert assignments with no reliability measure. The parameter space carries no class-level information, forcing the server to aggregate all clients uniformly and destroying the expert specialization built during local training. We call this class-level specialization invisibility. To address these problems, we propose FedEMoE. On the client side, Evidential Mixture-of-Experts equips router and experts with evidential heads, dynamically adjusts the number of active experts based on routing uncertainty, and compresses accumulated evidence into a per-client signature. On the server side, Evidence-Guided Class-Aware Aggregation takes the signatures as input and adaptively performs class-aware parameter fusion and component recombination. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and FEMNIST show that FedEMoE consistently outperforms eight baseline methods across all settings. Our code is available at https://github.com/Stephen-Chow1/FedEMoE-CIKM.

item.title: FedCGR: Federated Cross-Domain Generative Recommendation
item.description:
CIKM · Zhuodong Liu, Hugen Lv, Xiangyu Li, Bohan Guo, Peiyu Hu
Cross-domain recommendation (CDR) transfers preference knowledge across related domains, but federated deployment makes cross-domain alignment difficult because the behavioral anchors that align item spaces, such as overlapping users and shared interaction signals, are often sparse, unavailable, or privacy-sensitive across clients. To address this tension, we revisit federated CDR as generation over a stable semantic item language. By representing items as discrete semantic ID (SID) sequences derived from public item-side metadata, cross-domain item alignment is induced by a shared vocabulary rather than by exchanging private interactions or aligning domain-specific embeddings. Directly federating SID-based generators, however, introduces two design constraints: the SID tokenizer must remain fixed to preserve cross-client token consistency, which creates a semantic-only bottleneck because local collaborative filtering (CF) signals cannot be globally shared or aligned; meanwhile, standard federated averaging can cause negative transfer under domain heterogeneity. To overcome these constraints, we propose FedCGR, a federated generative CDR framework that keeps the item language stable and makes adaptation explicit. FedCGR injects local CF evidence through a reliability-aware semantic interface and trains a prototype-personalized generator that selectively aggregates shared parameters according to domain relatedness while keeping domain-specific quantities local. Experiments on six Amazon cross-domain scenarios show that FedCGR consistently outperforms federated generative baselines and achieves competitive performance against strong sequential and federated CDR methods under both full-ranking and sampled evaluation protocols. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/ZhuodLiu/FedCGR.

item.title: Dynamic Feature-Embedding Communication via Codebook Distillation for Federated Recommendation
item.description:
CIKM · Mingzhe Han, Jiahao Liu, Dongsheng Li, Jiankui Zhou, Yaqiong Li, Hansu Gu
Federated recommendation systems commonly protect user privacy by keeping user parameters on local devices, while exchanging item parameters for collaborative model training. However, such item parameters usually model items independently and suffer from both efficiency and effectiveness challenges, making communication costs grow with the item space and limiting cross-item generalization and robustness to noisy feedback. To address these limitations, we propose to model items via shared latent feature embeddings for communication. Residual Quantization (RQ) provides a natural way to instantiate this communication by representing each item with a short sequence of discrete code IDs, i.e., Semantic IDs (SIDs). However, directly applying centralized and static RQ-based recommendation to federated learning is non-trivial due to 1) private and biased historical interactions and 2) evolving collaborative information. We propose RQFedRec, an RQ-based federated recommendation framework for dynamic feature-embedding communication. To construct globally aligned codebooks without accessing private interactions, RQFedRec introduces an information distillation module. Each client first learns item embeddings that encode local collaborative information from private interactions, and then distills such information into feature-indexed codebooks under globally shared SIDs, making sparse and biased local signals more compatible with server aggregation. To adapt to evolving collaborative information, RQFedRec introduces a self-refining SID update module that dynamically refines global SID assignments from aggregated codebooks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RQFedRec improves recommendation performance and reduces communication costs without relying on semantic information, while further benefiting from public semantics when available. Code is available at https://github.com/Mingzhe-Han/RQFedRec.

item.title: FedHUR: Learning Hierarchical Utility-Guided Client Relations for Personalized Federated Recommendation
item.description:
CIKM · Mingzhe Han, Jiahao Liu, Dongsheng Li, Jiankui Zhou, Hansu Gu, Peng Zhang
Federated recommendation enables collaborative model training while keeping user interaction data on local clients. A central problem in federated recommendation is how to aggregate useful information across clients for personalized recommendation. Existing personalized aggregation methods usually construct client relations from predefined parameter-based assumptions, such as parameter similarity or complementarity, and use these relations to determine aggregation weights. However, such methods construct a single global relation, which is insufficient to capture the hierarchical and multi-granularity nature of user relations in recommendation. Moreover, these predefined relations cannot directly reflect whether the related clients can improve prediction performance after aggregation. To address these limitations, we propose FedHUR, a federated recommendation framework for learning hierarchical utility-guided client relations. FedHUR takes item-item filters as the object for relation construction and aggregation. Specifically, it first aggregates and clusters each client's local information to obtain global hierarchical information. Each client computes hierarchical utility signals based on its local information and the global hierarchical information, indicating which collaborative information is useful for improving its prediction. The server uses these utility signals to retrieve clients that are useful to that client for further personalized aggregation. Extensive experiments on five real-world datasets show that FedHUR consistently outperforms existing federated recommendation baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of hierarchical utility-guided client relation learning. Code is available at https://github.com/Mingzhe-Han/FedHUR.

item.title: Stitch the Fragments: One-Shot Hierarchical Federated Clustering
item.description:
CIKM · Shenghong Cai, Zihua Yang, Yuzhu Ji, Yiqun Zhang, Mengke Li, Yang Lu
Federated Clustering (FC) faces a critical bottleneck in real-world scenarios, i.e., global clusters are rarely intact, often fragmenting into incomplete, multi-granular unlabeled ''clusterlets'' distributed across Non-IID clients. Although hierarchical clustering is theoretically well-suited to model such nested distributions, its recursive nature strictly relies on multi-round communication, introducing prohibitive computational overhead and severe privacy vulnerabilities. This paper, therefore, proposes a novel one-shot hierarchical federated clustering framework designed to seamlessly ''stitch'' the fragmented local clusterlets into a holistic global distribution. Our approach enables clients to perform autonomous fine-grained distribution exploration, uploading prototype-level knowledge via a dynamic parameter-interleaving mechanism to scramble transmission trajectories, which effectively prevents the server from tracing individual client data distributions. Subsequently, a multi-granular learning mechanism at the server fuses these granularly inconsistent local clusterlets, reconstructing a coherent global hierarchy for ultimate clustering. Extensive experiments on real benchmark datasets illustrate the superiority of the proposed approach, which effectively bridges the granularity gap among heterogeneous clients while minimizing privacy exposure risks via anonymized informative one-shot communication.

item.title: FedMCS: Federated Multi-Granularity Chemical-Semantic Distillation for Molecular Graph Learning
item.description:
CIKM · Xingjie Zeng, Bin Xiong, Cheng Shi, Shuai Wang, Chong Zhang, Cheng Zhong
Federated molecular learning enables collaborative molecular property prediction across distributed institutions while keeping raw molecular graphs decentralized. However, most existing federated molecular methods transfer knowledge through shared parameters, whole-molecule representations, or label-dependent prototypes. This makes collaboration vulnerable to scaffold, domain, endpoint, and label-space heterogeneity. These coarse or task-bound signals struggle to capture chemical patterns that can be reused across clients while remaining consistent with each client's local prediction objective. To address these issues, we propose Federated Multi-granularity Chemical-Semantic Distillation (FedMCS), which builds a reusable substructure-level channel regularized by a fixed fingerprint prior. FedMCS summarizes client-side substructure embeddings as compact Gaussian prototypes, allowing recurring chemical motifs to serve as transferable carriers while raw molecular graphs and task heads remain local. A gate conditioned on a client-local task embedding selectively reuses refined global mean prototypes when the same fragment has different relevance across endpoints. On the server, Soft Chemical Distillation regularizes prototype relations with fingerprint-derived similarity, encouraging the shared prototype space to preserve a fingerprint-induced neighborhood structure. Experiments on eight MoleculeNet benchmarks show that FedMCS consistently outperforms federated baselines in intra-dataset scaffold non-IID settings and obtains the best weighted average among collaborative methods in the cross-dataset setting. These results support substructure prototypes as an effective transfer granularity for federated molecular learning.

item.title: DualFed-RCGC: Dual-Track Personalized Federated Learning via Covariance-Transferred Rare-Class Geometric Completion
item.description:
CIKM · Qianxin Li, Siyang Guo, Junbo Wang
Personalized federated learning under extreme data heterogeneity suffers from two coupled structural issues: local majority-class gradients contaminate the globally shared representation, while rare classes lack sufficient local support, making reliable local discrimination difficult. To address these issues, we propose DualFed-RCGC, a dual-track personalized federated learning framework. First, it employs a Y-shaped architecture with explicit gradient-path isolation, decoupling global representation learning from local adaptation to mitigate majority-dominated gradients from biasing the shared backbone. Second, to improve discrimination for underrepresented classes, we introduce a Covariance-Transferred Rare-Class Geometric Completion (RCGC) module. It calibrates local decision boundaries by synthesizing geometry-aware virtual features using fixed Equiangular Tight Frame (ETF) anchors and covariance structures transferred from local majority classes. Finally, a class-aware masked distillation strategy selectively injects global knowledge to further improve rare-class discrimination. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet demonstrate that DualFed-RCGC consistently improves personalized local accuracy while retaining a usable shared branch for federated aggregation.

item.title: Cross-Architecture Semantic Backdoor Attack in Data-Driven Federated Learning
item.description:
CIKM · Wei Hou, Yun Li, Ziye Zhu, Wenqiong Zhang
Traditional Federated Learning (FL) relies on iterative parameter exchange, which limits architectural flexibility and introduces high communication overhead for large foundation models. To address these issues, Data-Driven Federated Learning (DD-FL) has recently emerged as a scalable alternative. Instead of exchanging model parameters, DD-FL adopts a one-shot data-centric pipeline, where heterogeneous clients collaboratively annotate a shared unlabeled public dataset and the server performs knowledge distillation through soft-label aggregation. While DD-FL improves scalability and supports heterogeneous architectures, it also introduces a new attack surface on the shared public dataset. These public datasets are often collected from web crawlers or collaborative platforms with limited integrity validation, making data poisoning feasible. Moreover, since DD-FL removes parameter-level interactions and relies on soft-label aggregation across heterogeneous models, traditional FL backdoor attacks designed for individual models are easily diluted and exhibit poor cross-architecture transferability. In this paper, we propose a semantic backdoor attack for DD-FL. Our method generates poisoned samples by aligning image perturbations with target semantic directions in a shared vision-language space. This enables poisoned samples to induce semantically aligned target predictions across heterogeneous client models, making the backdoor more transferable during soft-label aggregation. We also study how biased aggregation weights further strengthen the attack effect. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and TinyImageNet show that our method achieves higher attack success rates and robustness than existing baselines, while maintaining high clean accuracy and strong visual stealthiness.

item.title: FedICL-KVc: Federated In-Context Learning via KV Cache
item.description:
CIKM · Yiming Chen, Nan He, Zheng Jiang, Lifeng Sun
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly constrained by the scarcity of high-quality public data, making private data essential for further improvement. However, private data is typically distributed across resource-constrained devices and cannot be shared due to strict privacy requirements, rendering conventional federated fine-tuning of LLMs impractical under limited computation and communication budgets. To address these challenges, we propose Federated In-Context Learning via KV Cache (FedICL-KVc), a novel framework that enables effective utilization of private data without parameter updates. Instead of transmitting raw demonstrations, clients upload only the corresponding key--value (KV) caches generated during auto-regressive inference, which are compact, smaller than full-model parameter payloads, and subject to an empirical reconstruction-risk evaluation under a restricted attack model. To further enhance efficiency and effectiveness, we introduce a confidence-based demonstration selection strategy to identify informative client samples, and a server-side KV cache compression method guided by a proxy dataset to reduce inference cost and suppress irrelevant information. Experiments on multiple tasks demonstrate that FedICL-KVc achieves competitive performance without client-side parameter updates or full-model parameter transmission while avoiding direct raw-data transmission.

item.title: FedPerGen: A Personalized Generative Augmentation Framework for Federated Recommendation
item.description:
CIKM · Tianzi Zang, Cheng Xu, Jiayi Sun, Mingyuan Gao, Yicong Li, Juan Li
Federated recommendation is an emerging paradigm that enables collaborative model training while preserving user privacy by keeping raw interaction data on local devices. However, in this setting, each client performs local training solely on a single user's limited historical interactions, which further exacerbates the data sparsity issue that has long been a bottleneck limiting recommendation performance. In this paper, we delve into the data sparsity problem in federated recommendation and propose FedPerGen, a personalized generative augmentation framework for federated recommendation. Specifically, each client is required to upload a user preference proxy to the server. The server then feeds this proxy along with diversity-constrained random noise into a generative network to synthesize personalized pseudo-item embeddings for each client. To ensure the informativeness and diversity of the generated embeddings, we design three complementary optimization objectives: feature-contrastive loss, model-alignment loss, and embedding-diversity loss. Furthermore, a two-stage warm-up training strategy is proposed to guarantee reliable user preference proxies and high-quality pseudo embeddings. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that FedPerGen consistently improves various federated recommendation baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/xcheng202202/FedPerGen .

item.title: FedHCA: Hierarchical Contribution-Aware Aggregation for Asynchronous Federated Class-Incremental Learning
item.description:
CIKM · Yan Duan, Xin Qin, Xiaodong Yang, Shubai Chen
Federated class-incremental learning (FCIL) aims to learn emerging classes across decentralized clients while preserving previously acquired knowledge. Existing FCIL methods are often designed or evaluated under relatively synchronous new-class exposure settings, while in realistic federated systems, a new class may initially appear on only a few clients with limited samples. This creates a local-global propagation mismatch: scarce new-class samples make local updates unstable, whereas majority-dominated aggregation dilutes these updates and slows the global propagation of new-class knowledge. To address this problem, we propose Hierarchical Contribution-Aware Aggregation (FedHCA), a novel framework for FCIL under asynchronous new-class exposure. FedHCA stabilizes local new-class update formation via a prototype-guided local learning strategy, and further promotes global new-class propagation through coarse-to-fine hierarchical aggregation. Specifically, the server first distinguishes new-class-exposed clients from old-class-only clients, then groups exposed clients according to their semantic and update-direction consistency, and finally performs contribution-weighted group aggregation based on update magnitudes. This design amplifies informative new-class updates while maintaining old-class stability. Experiments on CIFAR-100, CIFAR-10, and SVHN show that FedHCA achieves the best overall accuracy and a better balance between old-class retention and new-class adaptation compared with representative baselines. Further analyses confirm its propagation efficiency, component effectiveness, and robustness under asynchronous exposure.
